feedback: If a thin-skinned animal is sent into cold water, show it weakening and prompt: what feature would slow the body's heat from escaping? (blubber as insulation).
If a brightly coloured animal is spotted by predators, prompt: what feature would help it hide? (camouflage).
When a learner tries to add every feature to one animal, highlight that real animals are suited to particular seas and ask which feature best fits THIS challenge.
Reinforce correct links by restating the pairing as 'this feature helps because it solves [this challenge]', not as a feature the animal wanted.
activities.intendedInsight: Each adaptation answers a SPECIFIC environmental challenge; no single animal carries every possible adaptation (there is no all-purpose 'super-animal'). Learners reason from a problem to the body feature that solves it, and can transfer this reasoning to a new challenge.
learnerActions: Read a stated habitat challenge, e.g. a freezing polar ocean full of predators, or fast-moving prey to catch.
Choose features to fit onto a bare animal from a set: a layer of blubber, a streamlined shape, camouflage skin, suckered arms.
Predict, before checking, which features will help the animal survive this specific challenge and say why.

Run the outcome and observe the consequence of each choice: a thin-skinned animal weakens in cold water until blubber is added; a brightly coloured animal is spotted and chased until camouflage is used; a boxy body misses prey a streamlined one catches.
Solve several different seas (cold, predator-heavy, hunting), noticing that no single animal can carry every possible adaptation.
Given a brand-new environment (e.g. freezing water or hunting in the dark), predict a plausible adaptation and justify it from the challenge.
activities.title: Survive the sea: equip an animal to meet a challenge

feedback: If a learner says the fat heated the hand, point to the result: the fat was room temperature yet the insulated hand stayed comfortable longer, so the fat trapped the body's own heat rather than making heat.

If a learner says a seal grew blubber because it felt cold, separate one animal's life from change across many generations: an animal inherits its features from its parents (some, like a seal pup's blubber, build up as it grows), and better-suited animals survive and pass their features on. (Full natural selection comes later; here just block 'it changed itself because it needed to'.)
When a learner names a second adaptation, ask them to pair it with the specific challenge it solves (streamlined → swim fast to catch food or escape; camouflage → hide from predators).
activities.intendedInsight: Blubber is not itself warm and does not generate heat; it insulates by slowing heat loss. Different animals have different adaptations because they face different challenges.
learnerActions: Predict which hand will stay comfortable in a bowl of iced water: a hand inside an empty bag, or a hand inside an identical bag surrounded by solid fat/shortening. Say why before trying.

Dip both hands briefly and compare how well each keeps its warmth. Usually the fat-covered hand stays comfortable longer while the hand in the empty bag soon gets uncomfortable, even though the fat was never warmer than the hand. Exactly how it feels depends on how thick the fat is, how well it covers the hand, how cold the water is and how long the hands stay in.
Explain the result: the fat did not make heat; it slowed the body's own heat from escaping into the cold water — this is what blubber does for a seal.

Discuss follow-up puzzles: why a polar seal has blubber but a fast tuna is streamlined instead; where blubber comes from (seals inherit the ability to build blubber from their parents, and many pups are born quite thin and put it on by drinking rich milk; a seal does not grow blubber because it felt cold); and what challenge an anglerfish's glowing lure might solve.
activities.title: Blubber-glove investigation: insulation, not heat

feedback: Prompt the learner to tie any proposed feature back to the specific challenge it answers.
If reasoning stalls, offer a simpler contrast (cold vs needing speed) to re-anchor the challenge→feature logic.
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptations can be reasoned about from a challenge, and explaining the link out loud consolidates the problem→solution understanding.
learnerActions: Pose or respond to a survival puzzle, e.g. 'how might an animal survive the cold, or hunt in the dark?'
Propose a plausible adaptation and justify it by naming the challenge it solves.
Respond to follow-up questions that probe the reasoning (why this feature and not another for this environment).
activities.title: Ask a marine biologist: justify an adaptation

feedback: If a learner attributes the difference to size or colour, redirect attention to how water moves around the shape.
Connect back: streamlining answers the SPEED challenge, one of several different challenges different animals face.
activities.intendedInsight: A streamlined shape reduces resistance in water, which helps an animal move fast — one specific solution to the challenge of speed.
learnerActions: Compare how water flows around a streamlined body versus a boxy one and observe which moves more easily.
Explain why a streamlined shape helps a fast swimmer catch prey or escape predators.
activities.title: Enrichment: streamlined vs boxy in moving water
